questions.q: Which plant vascular tissue is primarily responsible for the transport of water and inorganic mineral ions from roots to leaves?
a: Xylem vessels
Phloem sieve tubes
Cortex parenchyma
Sclerenchyma fibers

questions.q: What tissue translocates organic assimilates (such as sucrose and amino acids) from source regions to sink regions in flowering plants?
a: Xylem tracheids
Phloem tissue (sieve tube elements and companion cells)
Cambium ring
Endodermis

questions.q: What is the primary physical driving force responsible for the bulk flow of water up xylem vessels during transpiration?
a: Root pressure driven by active salt pumping
Active contraction of xylem vessel walls
The transpiration pull created by negative pressure (tension) generated through water evaporation from leaf mesophyll cell walls
Osmotic pressure from companion cells

questions.q: What term describes the pathway of water movement across plant root tissues where water travels exclusively through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing plasma membranes?
a: Symplast pathway
Vacuolar pathway
Transmembrane pathway
Apoplast pathway

questions.q: What is the function of the Casparian strip in the root endodermis?
a: Blocking the apoplast pathway of water and mineral movement, forcing water and solutes to pass selectively through the plasma membrane of endodermal cells
Providing mechanical rigidity against soil compaction
Actively synthesizing sucrose for phloem transport
Producing root hairs for mineral absorption

questions.q: Which pathway of water movement involves water crossing cell membranes and moving through the cytoplasm and plasmodesmata from cell to cell?
a: Apoplast pathway exclusively
Symplast pathway
Extracellular bypass pathway
Cuticular evaporation pathway

questions.q: What forces account for the cohesion-tension theory of water transport in xylem vessels?
a: Repulsion between water and lignin
Active pumping of water by root cells
Hydrogen bonding between water molecules (cohesion) creating a continuous tensile column, and adhesion of water to hydrophilic xylem walls
High hydrostatic pressure generated in leaves pushing water down

questions.q: What phenomenon causes droplets of liquid water to be forced out of specialized marginal leaf pores (hydathodes) under conditions of high root pressure and low transpiration?
a: Transpiration pull
Guttation
Cavitation
Plasmolysis

questions.q: Which structural features of xylem vessel elements adapt them efficiently for bulk water transport?
a: Dead, hollow, lignified cells lacking end walls and protoplasts, forming continuous unbroken tubes
Living companion cells packed with numerous chloroplasts
Sieve plates with porous callose linings
Thin cellulose walls permeable to air bubbles

questions.q: What structural adaptations characterize phloem sieve tube elements?
a: Thick secondary walls impregnated with waterproof suberin
Living cells with reduced cytoplasm, lacking nuclei, and possessing perforated sieve plates at their end walls
Dead tracheids with bordered pits
Glandular epidermal cells secreting nectar

questions.q: What is the biological role of companion cells associated with phloem sieve tube elements?
a: Generating mechanical tension for xylem transport
Transporting water radially across root cortex
Providing metabolic support, ATP, and protein synthesis for adjacent anucleate sieve tube elements via numerous plasmodesmata
Absorbing sunlight for photosynthesis

questions.q: According to the mass flow hypothesis of phloem translocation, how are sugars moved from sources to sinks?
a: By simple diffusion down a concentration gradient over long distances
By active evaporation through leaf stomata
By active transport of water through xylem
By a hydrostatic pressure gradient generated by active loading of sucrose into sieve tubes at sources (raising pressure) and unloading at sinks (lowering pressure)

questions.q: What environmental factor causes stomata to close in order to conserve water during periods of severe drought?
a: Loss of turgor pressure in guard cells resulting from potassium ion efflux and subsequent osmotic water loss
Intense bright sunlight exposure
High internal carbon dioxide depletion
Elevated atmospheric oxygen levels

questions.q: Which laboratory instrument is standardly used to measure the rate of transpiration by tracking water uptake in a leafy shoot?
a: Potometer
Respirometer
Colorimeter
Centrifuge

questions.q: What structural modification in xerophytic plants (such as marram grass or cacti) helps reduce excessive transpiration?
a: Broad, thin leaves with large surface areas
Stomata located on upper leaf surfaces exposed to direct wind
Rolled leaves, sunken stomata in pits, thick waxy cuticles, and hairs trapping a humid boundary layer
Absence of any vascular tissue

questions.q: How do mineral ions such as nitrates and magnesium enter plant root hair cells from the soil?
a: Exclusively by simple passive diffusion
Exclusively by bulk flow through air spaces
By osmosis down a water potential gradient
By active transport against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP

questions.q: What causes guard cells to change shape and open stomatal pores when light is available?
a: Active transport of potassium ions ($K^+$) into guard cells lowers their water potential, causing water to enter by osmosis, making them turgid and bowing outward due to thicker inner walls
Photosynthesis consumes all water in the leaf
Guard cells lose turgor pressure and collapse inward
Temperature drops below freezing point

questions.q: What term describes the breakage of the water column inside xylem vessels under extreme tension, resulting in an air embolism?
a: Guttation
Cavitation
Plasmolysis
Translocation

questions.q: Which plant cell adaptation maximizes the surface area available for the absorption of water and mineral ions in roots?
a: Extensive leaf cuticle layers
Porous sieve plates
Root hair extensions of epidermal cells
Lignified xylem vessel pits

questions.q: What defines a plant 'sink' in the context of phloem translocation?
a: Any photosynthetic tissue producing excess sucrose
A root storage organ during early spring germination
The transpiring leaf surface
Any region of the plant that consumes or stores organic assimilates, such as growing roots, fruits, shoot tips, or tubers

questions.q: What is the primary chemical substance deposited in xylem cell walls that provides mechanical strength and waterproofs the tissue?
a: Lignin
Cellulose
Chitin
Pectin

questions.q: How does high wind speed (air movement) affect the transpiration rate of a mesophytic plant shoot?
a: It decreases transpiration by cooling the leaf surface
It increases transpiration by sweeping away water vapor accumulating in the boundary layer outside stomata, maintaining a steep water potential gradient
It stops transpiration completely by forcing stomata shut
It has zero effect on transpiration

questions.q: What is the physiological significance of translocation in phloem being bidirectional, unlike the unidirectional flow of xylem?
a: Phloem transports water upward while xylem transports sugars downward
Phloem can reverse direction to transport metabolic waste out of roots
Organic assimilates can be transported from source leaves either upward to growing shoot tips or downward to developing roots and storage organs depending on plant needs
Bidirectional flow is required for gaseous exchange

questions.q: What role do proton pumps ($H^+$-ATPases) play in the active loading of sucrose into companion cells in phloem source tissues?
a: Pumping sucrose molecules directly across lipid bilayers without energy
Creating a high concentration of water inside sieve tubes
Generating hydrogen ion gradients that drive co-transport of sucrose alongside $H^+$ ions via symport carrier proteins
Breaking down starch into glucose

questions.q: What is the primary source of energy driving the movement of water through the plant soil-plant-atmosphere continuum?
a: Solar energy driving evaporation of water from leaf cell walls (transpiration)
Cellular respiration releasing ATP in root cells
Photosynthetic light reactions in chloroplasts
Gravitational pull on root systems

questions.q: Which environmental condition would result in the highest rate of transpiration in a well-watered plant?
a: High humidity, low temperature, and darkness
Warm, dry, windy, and sunny conditions
Saturated soil with zero wind and freezing temperatures
Total darkness and high atmospheric pressure

questions.q: What structural adaptation helps hydrophytes (such as water lilies) survive in aquatic environments with low oxygen availability in mud?
a: Thick waxy cuticles and sunken stomata
Extensive aerenchyma tissue containing large air spaces for internal gas diffusion from leaves to roots
Densely lignified xylem vessels blocking all air
Absence of root systems entirely

questions.q: What happens to the rate of water uptake measured by a potometer if an electric fan is directed at the leafy shoot?
a: Uptake rate drops to zero immediately
Uptake rate remains constant
Uptake rate decreases due to cooling
Uptake rate increases significantly due to accelerated transpiration caused by boundary layer removal
